title: The Effectiveness of Multimedia Learning for Distance Education Toward Early Childhood Critical Thinking During the COVID-19 Pandemic
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether multimedia-based distance learning can improve early childhood critical thinking during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Indonesian schools shifted to remote instruction. The authors frame critical thinking as an important early skill and argue that conventional instruction is insufficient for supporting it in distance settings.

The intervention was an online, multimedia-supported science learning program delivered through Zoom and animated videos. Lessons emphasized concrete science phenomena such as rain and rainbows, and included teacher-guided discussion, question asking, problem solving, retelling, and concluding activities. The study used a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with 30 children aged 5–6 years from Al-Fikri Kindergarten in Bekasi, Indonesia, comparing a multimedia-learning group with a conventional learning group.

Results showed statistically significant gains in overall critical thinking and in each measured subskill: interpretation, analyzing, evaluating, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. The authors conclude that multimedia learning is effective for supporting early childhood critical thinking in distance education, especially when it uses child-friendly visual and audio-visual materials tied to science topics. They also note that the approach may help children engage more actively and understand abstract ideas through concrete representations.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with one group described in the abstract and a non-equivalent group design discussed later, but without clear randomization, control of confounds, or effect sizes. It is peer-reviewed, but credibility is limited by the small sample and design/reporting inconsistencies.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are statistically significant and appear substantial in raw score terms, but the study does not report an effect size and is limited to a small early-childhood sample in one setting. The practical impact is therefore promising but unclear for broader K-12 generalization.

interventions.use_case: Online multimedia-based instruction delivered via Zoom for early childhood science learning, using animated videos, discussion prompts, problem-solving tasks, and child presentations to support critical thinking during distance education.

finding.finding_summary: Multimedia-based distance learning produced a significant improvement in early childhood critical thinking after eight meetings. In the quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with n=30 children aged 5-6, mean critical thinking scores increased from 60.1 (SD=17.7) at pretest to 83.7 (SD=10.8) at posttest, with a paired t-test showing t=15.750, p=0.000.
finding.measure: Critical thinking questionnaire aligned to Facione-style subskills (interpretation, analyzing, evaluating, inference, explanation, self-regulation); pretest and posttest scores

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was implemented through science topics such as rain and rainbows, with children asked to observe phenomena, discuss them, ask questions, and draw conclusions. The paper reports significant gains on reasoning-related subskills embedded in the critical thinking instrument, including interpreting, analyzing, evaluating, inference, explanation, and self-regulation (all p=0.000).
finding.measure: Subscores on critical thinking items tied to science-themed phenomena and reasoning tasks
